claims.text: TGA can be used to study high-temperature oxidation behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys.
In situ XRD can be used to study high-temperature phase evolution in refractory high-entropy alloys.
TGA and in situ XRD can be coupled to monitor oxidation and phase stability simultaneously.
The combined method directly monitors oxidation-induced weight gain while simultaneously identifying phase transitions and protective oxide scales.
The starting material is a dense refractory high-entropy alloy produced by powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous microstructure.
Oxidation testing can be performed in flowing air at approximately 1000 °C.
Mass change and phase evolution can be monitored continuously during the same oxidizing exposure.
Real-time TGA and in situ XRD can be acquired together under controlled oxidizing conditions and controlled heating and cooling rates.
High-temperature oxidation forms protective oxide layers that modify the mass and structural state of the alloy.
Silicides, spinels, or Cr2O3-based phases are examples of the protective layers expected to form.
TGA tracks mass gain caused by oxygen uptake and thereby reflects oxidation kinetics.
In situ XRD identifies phases and detects phase transitions or newly formed oxide phases.
Simultaneous TGA and XRD measurements enable direct correlation of oxidation kinetics with phase stability.
The oxidation experiment will produce a parabolic mass-gain curve.
A parabolic mass-gain curve corresponds to formation of a stable protective oxide scale.
At room temperature, the alloy undergoes negligible oxidation and retains its initial phase composition.
Rapid oxidation and scale spallation can limit the effectiveness of the combined method.
Insufficient instrumental resolution can prevent detection of minor or rapidly transforming phases.
Detection and quantification of subtle or minor oxide phases are instrument-dependent.
